Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: São Tomé and Príncipe has implemented DHIS2 as its national health information system, with individual tracker modules for primary health care (PHC) patient registry and consultations since 2020, supported by WHO and UNDP (tablets provided). Training occurs at facility level. However, pre-DHIS2 systems were mostly paper-based with parallel subsystems. A 2023 WHO EMTCT assessment (for HIV/syphilis) confirms rural health posts and primary centers use manual registries, patient cards, and paper aggregation sent upward; DHIS2 used at district level for aggregates, not routine facility digital entry. No direct evidence of digital patient records (registers, prescriptions) at rural clinics; likely paper collection with later digital entry at higher levels, fitting score 2 (predominantly paper with some digital/aggregate reporting). Recent (2025) efforts assess longitudinal records, but point-of-care remains paper-dominant per latest facility-specific report.

revision_notes: Original Value Code recorded 1 (Entirely paper) despite the row's own Comments arguing for score 2. Verified original sources (WHO DHIS2 results report 2020, WHO EMTCT assessment April 2023, dhis2.org July 2025 update) plus a fetched UNDP MPTF Joint Programme final narrative report (2023) confirming DHIS2 tablets/computers used for facility-level data entry in specific programmes (vaccination, HIV, TB, malaria). The 2023 WHO EMTCT assessment specifically addresses rural health posts/primary centres and documents manual registries/patient cards as the primary recording method, with DHIS2 aggregation occurring at district level rather than routine facility digital entry. Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), matching the evidence and the row's own analysis. Year set to 2023 based on the WHO EMTCT assessment, the most specific and authoritative rural-facility source.
revised_comments: São Tomé and Príncipe's Ministry of Health has rolled out DHIS2 nationally, with tablets and computers issued to health facilities and staff trained to enter data for specific programmes (COVID-19 vaccination, HIV, TB, malaria, immunisation) directly at the point of care. However, a 2023 WHO assessment of rural health posts and primary health centres finds that routine patient registration, consultations and prescriptions are still recorded in manual registers and patient cards, with paper aggregates sent upward for entry into DHIS2 at district level rather than routine digital capture at the facility itself. Rural clinics therefore combine predominantly paper-based record keeping with some genuine digital data capture for specific vertical health programmes.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case management in rural police stations of Sao Tome and Principe. A national Integrated Case Management System (ICMS) contract was awarded in Dec 2022, with phase 1 rollout planned for police, prosecution, judiciary, and prisons in the city of Sao Tome only (urban), with later expansion nationwide planned but no confirmed progress or rural implementation as of 2026. US State Dept reports and other sources describe police as ineffective/corrupt but silent on recording methods; likely paper-based dockets (procès-verbaux) in rural areas given small scale and lack of mentions.

revision_notes: Value Code 1 confirmed. Two of the three originally cited sources (US State Dept human rights report PDF, OSAC report) returned errors (403 forbidden) on fetch and could not be verified; retained the working Synisys source and added two newly verified sources in its place. Searches found an Integrated Case Management System (ICMS) contract (Dec 2022) rolling out only in São Tomé city, a 2023 report on the 'Zulu' national police informatisation programme (still in development), a 2024 PNSTP-UNITEL protocol for future digital services adoption, and a January 2026 UNODC equipment donation to the Polícia Judiciária headquarters (an urban, specialist investigative unit). No evidence found of digitisation in rural police stations; paper-based dockets remain the norm. Year set to 2026 based on the newest relevant source (UNODC donation), though it concerns urban investigative police rather than rural stations directly, hence medium confidence.
revised_comments: Digitalisation of case records in São Tomé and Príncipe's justice and security sector remains concentrated in the capital. An Integrated Case Management System (ICMS/Synergy eCase), contracted in December 2022, has its first phase limited to police, prosecution, judiciary and prisons within the city of São Tomé, with nationwide rural rollout still only an aspiration. A January 2026 donation of computers and secure data storage from UNODC went to the Polícia Judiciária's headquarters for criminal investigation work, again an urban, specialist unit rather than rural police stations. No evidence has been found of digital case recording in rural police stations, which continue to rely on paper dockets (registos/boletins de ocorrência).

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices (Postos de Registo Civil) in Sao Tome and Principe predominantly use paper forms for birth registration, with high coverage (98% rural births registered per 2023 UN/World Bank data via campaigns). Electronic databases exist only in urban areas. Local rural offices send paper copies to regional offices for electronic processing and transmission to central DGRN. Digitization efforts ongoing (pilots for MOSIP digital ID anchored on CRVS since 2024, World Bank project strategy), but rural facilities remain paper-based with some digital aggregation upstream. Score 2 reflects predominant paper at rural points with partial digital backend.

revision_notes: Original Value Code recorded 1 (Entirely paper) despite the row's own Comments arguing for score 2. Verified the cited UNECA/AfDB CRVS digitalisation report, the BiometricUpdate June 2025 MOSIP pilot article, and the DGRN 'about' page. A 2018 academic paper on STP's SIGA system confirms that, historically, civil registration was collected on paper at district level and digitised retrospectively at the centre. However, a directly quoted March 2026 statement from the DGRN's chief civil registrar (Idalécio Silveira) describes current practice of registering births directly into an electronic database at maternities nationwide, phasing out paper forms, alongside a March 2025 report of a new integrated registry management system and a MOSIP digital ID pilot. This is stronger and more recent evidence than the original sources supported, and moves the facility-level status beyond 'mostly paper' to 'mostly digital - some paper' (3), reflecting the shift to point-of-registration electronic capture for births (the dominant vital event) while other registry acts likely retain more paper use. Year set to 2026 based on the newest, most specific dated source.
revised_comments: Civil registration in São Tomé and Príncipe is shifting from a purely paper-based process towards direct electronic capture at the point of registration. The Direcção-Geral dos Registos e do Notariado (DGRN) reports that trained registry staff and midwives now register births directly into an electronic database at maternities across the country, with paper forms being phased out, and a new integrated management and identification system (backed by SIGA and a MOSIP-based digital ID pilot) has been rolled out since 2025. Older civil registry offices historically relied entirely on paper books, which were digitised retrospectively at the centre, so some paper-based processes for other vital events, such as deaths and marriages, persist alongside the newer electronic birth-registration workflow, placing the facility-level status as mostly digital with some continuing paper use.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Sao Tome and Principe has implemented an integrated Education EMIS system at the Department of Education level, supporting evidence-based policymaking and data management. However, no specific details found on rural primary schools using digital tools for attendance, enrollment, grades, or admin data. Given rural infrastructure challenges and lack of school-level digital mentions, processes are likely predominantly paper-based with some aggregation into central digital EMIS.

revision_notes: Original Value Code recorded 1 (Entirely paper) despite the row's own Comments arguing for a mixed/score 2 status. Verified the cited UNESCO IICBA brief; the Planipolis link resolved only to a country navigation page with no facility-level detail, and the Education Profiles inclusion page covers special education policy rather than digitisation. Found and read a World Bank Quality Education for All Project completion report confirming that, by project close, 66 of 88 primary schools had received a computer and internet connection with head teachers and staff trained to enter data directly into the national EMIS/SIGE at school level, and a 2023 GPE-supported sector assessment confirming that many schools - constrained by lack of electricity, computers or internet, or difficulty using SIGE - still do not use the system. Given rural schools are disproportionately affected by these infrastructure gaps, recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), consistent with the row's own analysis. Year set to 2023 based on the GPE sector assessment, the most specific recent source on facility-level EMIS usage barriers.
revised_comments: São Tomé and Príncipe operates a national Education Management Information System (SIGE/EMIS), and a World Bank-supported programme has equipped a majority of primary schools with computers and internet connectivity, training head teachers and administrative staff to enter attendance, enrolment and administrative data directly at school level. However, a 2023 assessment for the Global Partnership for Education finds that many schools, disproportionately those in rural areas, are still unable to use SIGE because they lack electricity, computers or reliable internet, or because staff find the system difficult to use, meaning rural primary schools combine predominantly paper-based record keeping with partial digital data entry where infrastructure allows.
